name: Ziryab depilatories

lead: Ziryab was a 9th-century musician and tastemaker at the court of Cordoba in Al-Andalus, credited in later accounts with spreading many grooming habits. Wikipedia's hair-removal article says chemical depilatories for women were introduced in 9th-century Al-Andalus by him, though it marks the claim as uncited.
The appeal was smooth, hair-free skin without shaving. The Ziryab article itself does not mention depilatories, only shaving, haircuts, a deodorant and an early toothpaste.

paras: Details of the products are not recorded in the accounts consulted. Depilatories in general are creams or pastes applied and wiped off.
Chemical depilatories can burn or irritate skin, and ancient formulas sometimes included harsh or toxic ingredients such as orpiment (arsenic trisulfide) in lime pastes used historically elsewhere.

angle.text: The attribution concerns women's hair removal for smooth skin; specifics of the products are not documented.

lead: Ziryab (9th century) is remembered as a trendsetter at the Umayyad court in Al-Andalus, credited with popularising face shaving, new short haircuts with straight bangs, a deodorant, an early toothpaste, and twice-daily bathing.[1] Many of these claims are hedged ("said to", "thought to") and the article carries an accuracy-dispute tag; much of the material traces to a Saudi Aramco World article by Robert Lebling.[1]

Separately, the hair-removal article states that chemical depilatories for women were introduced in 9th-century Al-Andalus by Ziryab, noting that this claim lacks a citation.[2] The Ziryab article does not mention depilatories.[1]

paras: The claim appears in a general history of hair removal, which also covers ancient Greek and Roman depilatories, Egyptian depilation and the slaked lime, ash and orpiment paste used since antiquity.[2]

Ziryab is credited with shaving among men, the straight-fringe haircut leaving ears and neck free, and replacing rose-water hair washing with salt and fragrant oils.[1] The claim that he opened beauty parlours for elite women is not supported by early sources.[1]

timeline.event: Chemical depilatories for women said to be introduced in Al-Andalus by Ziryab.[2]
